"It's not done in a detached, in an arms-length way. It’s actually done in a very physical way."
The company sends team members to meet photographers directly, from large international events to smaller studio visits where they can understand professional workflows in detail.
Orta gives an example and explains that Capture One team members recently visited studios in Paris to hear how photographers work and what challenges they face.
Those conversations help shape future products and services.
"We have an abundance of touch points that allow us to incorporate and understand what our customers need, but also how the industry is evolving," he says.
"The technology almost seems to melt away"
One area where Capture One sees continued importance is tethered shooting – a workflow where a camera is connected directly to a computer during a shoot, enabling images to appear instantly on a larger display.
Capture One says tethering remains a key part of professional photography, particularly when teams are collaborating on commercial shoots.
"It's such a central part of the Capture One experience," says Orta.
“You can have a team of people working around a photography shoot and the camera is connected to a workstation, and that immediately brings that team into the process.”
For Orta, the best technology is often the technology photographers barely notice.
"What we see is that the technology almost seems to melt away into the background," he explains.
"People start to talk about their photography and where they want to get to, and how they get to the creative vision that they have."
Capture One has committed to releasing tethering support for Hasselblad cameras before the end of the year, with the focus on reliability, speed and stability.
"The things that we care about are the speed of the file transfer and the reliability of that connection," says Orta.
"The day that we launch tethering, photographers will just be able to pick up their body, plug their cable there, and it’s just going to work seamlessly."
Although Capture One is headquartered in Denmark with a team of around 122 people, the company also has offices in Greece, London and the US. Orta says the company’s influence reaches far beyond its size.
"We're this very, very specialized, very focused company from Denmark, but the impact that we have on global photography vastly outsizes the fact that we’re this specialized company," he says.
Capture One software is used across commercial photography, fashion, advertising, journalism, entertainment and other areas where images play an important cultural and commercial role.
Sometimes, Orta says, the company even notices its software appearing unexpectedly in films and television shows during photography scenes.
"It's something that is very, very unique to a company that has achieved this status and this position as an industry standard," he says.
For Capture One, the future of photography is not just about new technology – it is about continuing to support the people creating the images.
"We always do that in a very close relationship with our customers," Orta says.
"That's how we influence the way photography workflow works."

The company behind one of the world’s most-downloaded creative apps just made it possible to launch a virtual personality in the time it takes to scroll through a filter menu.
Every Persona character starts as a single design then gets animated, restyled, and reused across an entire content calendar.
There’s a particular kind of fatigue that’s settled over social media in the last couple of years. Everyone is a “creator” now, everyone is expected to be on camera, and the algorithm rewards the people willing to show up every single day with a fresh face, a fresh outfit, and a fresh reason to be interesting. It’s exhausting even to watch, let alone do. Picsart, with more than 130 million monthly active users and over 2.5 billion lifetime downloads, is betting that a lot of people would rather build a character to do that work for them.
Launched in early March 2026, Persona is Picsart’s entry into what the company is calling the “faceless creator” economy a corner of the internet where the account behind the avatar, the mascot, or the animated alter ego might never appear on camera at all, and audiences increasingly don’t seem to mind. Picsart is chasing a genuinely enormous opportunity here: it’s pointing to a $40 billion influencer marketing industry and a $750 billion universe of small businesses and solo entrepreneurs who need a consistent online presence but don’t necessarily have the time, the budget, or the desire to build one in front of a camera.
Picsart’s existing scale is the launchpad Persona is built on top of.
Strip away the marketing language and Persona is, at its core, a character generator that doesn’t stop at a single static image. You pick a “vibe”, a curated aesthetic rather than a blank prompt box and the tool builds a character around it. That’s a meaningfully different starting point than most AI image generators, which hand you a text field and expect you to already know how to describe cheekbone structure or lighting temperature in a way the model understands. Persona flips that: choose a look, and the tool handles the interpretation.
From there, the character stops being a single frame and becomes something closer to a digital cast member. Persona’s motion tools convert that static design into short video clips, formatted and ready for TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts the three places short-form video actually lives. And crucially, the character it creates isn’t a one-off. The same face, the same proportions, the same visual signature can be pulled back up for the next post, restyled with a new outfit through image-to-image editing, and dropped into a new scene without being rebuilt from scratch. Picsart’s own framing for this is “create once, reuse everywhere,” which is really the heart of the pitch: this isn’t a novelty generator for a single viral image, it’s meant to be the engine behind an ongoing account.
The range of characters on offer is wider than you might expect from a tool aimed at influencer marketing. Persona supports realistic human avatars down to details like freckles and skin texture alongside animals, aliens, fantasy creatures, and stylized mascots. That’s a deliberate choice. Picsart isn’t only picturing a single archetype of AI influencer; it’s picturing pet accounts, fantasy world-building creators, brand mascots that need a consistent face across a marketing campaign, and everyday creators who simply don’t want to be recognized.
Under the hood, Picsart says the platform automatically routes each generation request to whichever underlying AI video model is best suited for the job, spanning a range that includes tools like Veo 3.1 and Kling 3.0. For the average user, that’s meant to be invisible; you’re not supposed to need to know or care which model is doing the rendering. You’re supposed to just get a good clip.
Picsart isn’t a startup fumbling toward relevance here, it’s a company with a genuine, long-running foothold in the creative tools space, and Persona is arriving as part of a deliberate pattern rather than a one-off experiment. It follows a string of recent AI-forward launches from the company, including Aura, Flow, and an AI Assistant, each one pushing the platform further from “photo editor” and closer to a full AI content studio. Persona reads as the next, more ambitious step in that progression: rather than helping someone touch up a photo they already took, the company is now helping them build a personality that didn’t exist an hour ago.
It’s a telling line, because it frames Persona less as a fun AI toy and more as infrastructure, a way to remove the friction between having an idea for content and actually having something postable. For a certain kind of creator, that friction has always been the real bottleneck: not a lack of ideas, but the logistics of filming, editing, appearing, and doing it again tomorrow.
It’s worth being specific about who Picsart is building this for, because “AI influencer generator” can sound like a niche gimmick if you don’t picture the actual use cases. There’s the aesthetic character creator who wants a consistent, stylized persona for a lifestyle or fashion-adjacent account, without necessarily wanting to be the one on camera every day. There’s the pet-influencer space, which has quietly become one of the more lucrative and durable corners of social media, and which Persona can now serve with characters that don’t require an unusually photogenic or cooperative animal. There’s the small business owner who needs a friendly, recognizable brand mascot to appear consistently across a marketing calendar, without hiring a designer for every single asset. And there’s the simple camera-shy creator, someone with real expertise or a real point of view, who has been kept off platforms that reward video specifically because they don’t want to be recognized, or filmed, or judged on their appearance rather than their content.
That last group might end up being the most significant one. Faceless content isn’t a new idea; voiceover-driven explainer channels and text-on-screen accounts have existed for years but it’s historically been visually limited compared to accounts with an actual human presenting. Persona is a direct attempt to close that gap: give the faceless creator a face anyway, just one that belongs to a character rather than a person.
Picsart is making Persona available across web, iOS, Android, and Windows, and the company says it’s also built to work alongside the AI tools people are already using day to day, including ChatGPT, Claude, and various terminal-based AI workflows an acknowledgment that most creators today aren’t operating inside a single app, but are stitching together ideas, scripts, and assets across several tools before anything gets posted.
There’s an obvious question sitting underneath all of this, and it’s not really about Picsart: it’s about what happens to the idea of an “influencer” once the influencer doesn’t have to be a person at all. Virtual influencers aren’t new brands that have experimented with fully synthetic personalities for the better part of a decade but they’ve mostly required real production budgets and specialized studios to pull off convincingly. What Persona is proposing is much more democratized: put that same capability into a consumer app that already has well over a hundred million people opening it every month, and let anyone with an idea and a few minutes try it.
Whether that leads to a wave of genuinely compelling new characters or a flood of interchangeable AI avatars is the kind of thing only the next year of actual usage will answer. But Picsart is clearly betting that the appetite is there for creators who are tired of being the product, and for audiences who, it turns out, may be perfectly happy following a character as long as the character is consistent, well-made, and shows up on time.
Persona is live now at picsart.com, alongside Picsart’s existing suite of editing and AI content tools.

Great tools amplify your creativity while allowing you to focus on your ideas. That's been our focus since Photoshop's earliest days, and it’s what drives us today, especially as AI reshapes what's possible in creative work.
Today, we're introducing a new set of Photoshop innovations to give you more choice in how you create, more flexibility in how you work, and more control over your results. Whether you're refining details with precision tools or exploring ideas through prompts, these updates are designed to help you work with greater efficiency and confidence so you can stay focused on your creative vision from start to finish.
More precision, less friction, greater creative control
As a creative professional, your time is your critical resource, and you want technology that streamlines the busywork without sacrificing the discretion and judgment that defines your craft.
Light Adjustment Layer gives you professional-grade lighting controls — Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, and Blacks — in a new non-destructive adjustment layer, so you get Camera Raw-level results without ever leaving your Photoshop layers workflow.
Instruct Edit with Masks , powered by Firefly Image 5, understands the full context of your image so you no longer need to precisely mark every edit area yourself. Just describe the precise edits you’re looking for — such as opening closed eyes or placing a hat on a specific person’s head — with simple prompts. The unmasked areas remain untouched so your other important elements, like faces, logos, or brand assets, are protected.
Markup lets you visually communicate edits by drawing directly on an image to show the model what you want — select areas to recolor, sketch arrows to indicate position, or brush in rough shapes to suggest new elements — so you can get results that more closely match your vision while reducing the ambiguity of text-only prompts.
Dynamic Text, Shapes and Paths extends Photoshop's Dynamic Text to any custom shape or path, allowing text to adapt automatically along curves and freeform layouts so you keep your formatting without manual rework.
Stock Panel Integration puts more than 900 million Adobe Stock assets right inside Photoshop in a dockable panel, so you can easily discover, preview, and use assets without leaving your workflow.
Everyone moves from idea to execution in different ways, which is why we're adding more choice by bringing in a new optional space in Photoshop to try prompt-based editing outside the familiar Pro Editor workflow.
The AI Assisted Editor, now in beta, gives you the option of using a dedicated interface and natural-language prompt bar alongside popular generative tools powered by leading AI models, so you can explore ideas and make edits using simple prompts.
Prompt to Edit: Transform images using natural language prompts without complex manual editing.
Remove Background: Erase backgrounds, refine edges, and customize images in just a few clicks.
Generative Expand: Extend image dimensions and generate content that blends naturally with your composition.
Remove Tool: Eliminate unwanted objects and distractions while maintaining realistic image quality.
Generative Fill: Add, replace, or remove content using simple text prompts.
Generative Upscale: Increase image resolution while preserving sharpness and visual fidelity.
AI Markup: Annotate images to communicate edits visually and generate more precise results.
Prefer to keep working in the Pro Editor? Prompt to Edit offers the same natural language editing directly in the Pro Editor's Contextual Task Bar, so you can transform an entire image using simple prompts, with no selection required, right from the context bar you’re already using. Every Prompt to Edit result becomes a generative layer in your layer stack, so your edits stay organized and non-destructive
Whether you prefer prompts, precision tools, or a combination of both, Photoshop offers the flexibility to support the way you create.

Why you’re seeing Camera Raw updates more often
If you’ve been following Adobe’s release notes recently, you may have noticed something a little unusual. Camera Raw is now receiving updates every month, while the Lightroom apps continue on their regular two-month-ish release schedule.
That means you’ll sometimes see exciting new editing features announced for Camera Raw weeks—or even months—before they arrive in Lightroom. Naturally, that raises the question… why?
Although Camera Raw and Lightroom are different applications, they share the same editing engine. New editing features—such as AI tools, masking improvements, and new adjustment controls—are developed in Camera Raw before being adopted by the Lightroom apps.
Think of Camera Raw as Adobe’s workshop for new editing features. Once those tools are ready, the Lightroom team integrates them into Lightroom Classic, Lightroom Desktop, Lightroom Mobile, and Lightroom on the web.
Camera Raw has a much narrower role. It focuses almost entirely on developing and editing photos inside Photoshop and Bridge.
Lightroom, on the other hand, has a lot more moving parts. Along with photo editing, Adobe also has to consider:
Because there are more pieces that all need to work together, Lightroom releases naturally take longer to prepare.
Adobe’s intention is for editing features developed in Camera Raw to eventually make their way into Lightroom. However, there’s no guarantee every feature will appear in the very next Lightroom release.
Sometimes a feature needs additional work before it fits naturally into Lightroom’s workflow. Occasionally, Adobe may decide a feature isn’t the right fit for Lightroom at all.
Monthly Camera Raw releases also bring support for newly released cameras and lenses.
Support for newly released cameras and lenses often arrives in Camera Raw first. Lightroom users typically receive that same support in the next scheduled Lightroom release.
Even if you never use Camera Raw, understanding its release schedule helps explain why some editing features appear there before they arrive in Lightroom.
Just remember that “coming to Camera Raw” doesn’t necessarily mean “arriving in the next Lightroom release.”
Camera Raw’s monthly updates mean Adobe can introduce new editing technology sooner, while giving the Lightroom team time to integrate those features into the Lightroom apps.
So the next time you spot an exciting Camera Raw feature that isn’t yet available in Lightroom, don’t panic—you haven’t missed an update. Camera Raw is simply leading the way, giving Adobe the opportunity to develop and refine new editing tools before bringing many of them to the Lightroom apps.
If you want to try these features out in Camera Raw and have access to Photoshop, you can Open as Smart Object in Photoshop and use Camera Raw as a Filter. Of course, the photo will come back into Lightroom as a TIFF or PSD, rather than a raw file.

title: Adobe перевела Camera Raw на щомісячні релізи: нові фічі з'являються раніше за Lightroom
lead: Lightroom Queen пояснює: Camera Raw тепер оновлюється щомісяця, тоді як Lightroom залишається на приблизно двомісячному циклі, тож нові інструменти редагування з'являються в ACR на тижні або місяці раніше.
full: Camera Raw і Lightroom мають спільний двигун редагування, але нові функції — AI-інструменти, покращення масок, нові коригування — розробляються спочатку в Camera Raw, який має вужчу роль (проявка всередині Photoshop і Bridge). Lightroom має більше залежностей (Classic, Desktop, Mobile, web), тому його релізи готуються довше.

Adobe планує переносити функції з ACR у Lightroom, але без гарантії, що це буде в найближчому релізі; деякі фічі потребують доопрацювання або взагалі не потрапляють у Lightroom. Щомісячні релізи ACR також першими отримують підтримку нових камер і об'єктивів.
means: Для конкурентної розвідки це означає, що майбутні фічі Lightroom треба відстежувати за релізами Camera Raw — там вони з'являються на 1–2 місяці раніше. Це дає команді Luminar Neo більше часу оцінити, чи перетинається новинка з Mask AI, Noiseless AI або Relight AI, і підготувати відповідь до того, як фіча дійде до масової аудиторії Lightroom.

title: Apple представила Mac mini на M6 і M5 Pro: до 2,1x швидша обробка зображень
lead: Apple анонсувала Mac mini з новими чипами M6 (від $899) і M5 Pro (від $1699); передзамовлення з 25 серпня, поставки з 22 вересня. Apple заявляє суттєвий приріст у LLM-обробці та роботі з зображеннями.
